cloze.text: In health, the intact gingival margin is positioned {{c1::1 to 2 mm}} {{c2::coronal}} to the CEJ.
Attached gingiva is the part of the gingiva that is firm, dense and tightly connected to the {{c1::cementum or alveolar bone}}; it is not measured on the {{c2::palate}}.
Probe with walking (bobbing) strokes about {{c1::1 mm}} apart, kept parallel to the {{c2::long axis of the tooth}}; record the {{c3::deepest}} reading in each segment.
In the col area the probe is {{c1::slanted}} for better access, then straightened.
A periodontal pocket involves {{c1::apical}} movement of the junctional epithelium with {{c2::vertical}} bone loss.
A three-wall defect is bordered by {{c1::three osseous surfaces and one tooth surface}}.
Of the three bony defects, the {{c1::three-wall}} defect has the best prognosis.
A two-wall defect is bordered by {{c1::two osseous surfaces and two tooth surfaces}}.
A one-wall defect is bordered by {{c1::one osseous surface and three tooth surfaces}}.
In a {{c1::suprabony}} pocket the base of the pocket is {{c2::coronal to (above)}} the alveolar crest; it is typically associated with {{c3::horizontal}} bone loss.
cloze.extra: Supra- = above. Horizontal: bone reduced fairly uniformly across the tooth surface.

cloze.text: In an {{c1::infrabony}} pocket the base of the pocket is {{c2::apical to (below)}} the alveolar crest, within the bone defect; it is typically associated with {{c3::vertical (angular)}} bone loss.
cloze.extra: Infra- = below. Vertical loss is uneven and creates a trench-like defect alongside the root.

cloze.text: Recession: the free gingival margin is {{c1::apical}} to the CEJ, exposing the root surface.
Exposed root surface is more susceptible to {{c1::caries and abrasion}} than enamel, and root exposure aggravates {{c2::dentinal sensitivity}}.
Causes of recession include {{c1::frenal pull}} and {{c2::improper brushing and flossing technique}}.
When inflammation is present, gentle probing bleeds because the pocket is {{c1::ulcerated}} (not because the hygienist was too rough); bleeding is charted as a {{c2::red dot}}.
Absence of bleeding on probing is a predictor of periodontal {{c1::stability}}, but it does not guarantee the complete absence of disease.
Pale yellow pus ({{c1::purulence}}) represents an {{c2::active infection}}.
Horizontal tooth mobility is assessed by pushing the tooth in a {{c1::facial-lingual}} direction using two {{c2::blunt ends of dental instrument handles}}.
Vertical tooth mobility is assessed by {{c1::depressing the tooth into its socket}} with the blunt end of an instrument handle.
Miller class {{c1::I}} mobility: facial-lingual horizontal displacement of {{c2::up to 1 mm}}.
Miller class {{c1::II}} mobility: facial-lingual horizontal displacement {{c2::greater than 1 mm, up to 2 mm}}.
Miller class {{c1::III}} mobility: horizontal displacement {{c2::more than 2 mm}} and/or {{c3::vertical displacement (depression into the socket)}}.
Fremitus is assessed by placing a gloved {{c1::index finger}} against the {{c2::facial}} aspect of the tooth while the patient {{c3::taps the teeth together}}.
The presence and extent of furcation involvement is assessed with a {{c1::furcation probe}}.
Mandibular molars are usually {{c1::bifurcated}}, with {{c2::mesial and distal}} roots.
Maxillary molars are usually {{c1::trifurcated}}, with {{c2::mesiobuccal, distobuccal and palatal}} roots.
cloze.extra: Furcation entrances: facial, mesial and distal.

cloze.text: Maxillary first premolars can have bifurcated roots ({{c1::buccal and palatal}}).
Glickman class {{c1::I}} furcation: the curvature of the concavity can be detected with the probe tip but the probe {{c2::cannot enter the space}}; no radiolucency on radiographs.
Glickman class {{c1::II}} furcation: the probe penetrates the furcation {{c2::more than 1 mm}} but does not pass completely through; slight radiolucency may be visible.
Glickman class {{c1::III}} furcation: the probe {{c2::passes completely through}} the furcation; radiolucency is usually visible on radiographs.
Glickman class {{c1::IV}} furcation: the furcation entrance is {{c2::clinically visible}} and the probe passes completely through; larger radiolucency on radiographs.
Plaque is identified with {{c1::disclosing solution}} or by moving the tip of an instrument along the gingival margin; assess its location, thickness and presence/absence.
Plaque is the {{c1::primary etiology}} of gingivitis and periodontitis, so its level and location are assessed to improve home care.
Every calculus surface is covered with plaque because calculus is {{c1::porous}}.
CAL is measured from a fixed point, the {{c1::CEJ}}, so it is the most accurate assessment of periodontal support; probing depth is measured from the fluctuating {{c2::gingival margin}}.
Calculating CAL requires two measurements: {{c1::probing depth}} (gingival margin to base of pocket) and {{c2::gingival margin to CEJ}}.
When the gingival margin is coronal to the CEJ (health or hyperplasia/overgrowth): CAL = probing depth {{c1::minus}} GM-to-CEJ.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: gum covering the CEJ is hiding part of the root from your probing depth → SUBTRACT.

cloze.text: When the gingival margin is apical to the CEJ (recession): CAL = probing depth {{c1::plus}} GM-to-CEJ.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: gum has moved away from the CEJ, exposing root → ADD the exposed portion.

cloze.text: A dehiscence may be {{c1::one or two millimeters}} long or extend the full length of the root.
The three features of dehiscence are {{c1::gingival recession}}, {{c2::alveolar bone loss}} and {{c3::root exposure}}.
A fenestration is distinguished from a dehiscence because it is bordered by alveolar bone along its {{c1::coronal}} aspect.
The normal alveolar crest is about {{c1::1–2 mm}} {{c2::apical}} to the CEJ.
The alveolar crest is the {{c1::first}} area involved in bone destruction; {{c2::fuzziness}} (blunting) at the crest of the interdental bone helps confirm periodontal disease.
The lamina dura appears dense and continuous in {{c1::health}} and {{c2::thin or absent}} in disease.
Bone loss is measured from the {{c1::CEJ}} to the {{c2::alveolar crest}}.
{{c1::Horizontal}} bone loss is the most common pattern; it is associated with {{c2::suprabony}} defects, and the CEJ-to-CEJ line of adjacent teeth is {{c3::parallel}} to the alveolar crest.
{{c1::Vertical}} bone loss runs in an {{c2::oblique}} direction; the CEJ-to-CEJ line of adjacent teeth is NOT parallel to the alveolar crest.
{{c1::Periapical images}} or {{c2::vertical bitewings}} are used to assess bone level and other periodontal problems.
High kVp produces a {{c1::longer}} scale of contrast (many shades of gray) and is often preferred for detecting periodontal disease.
A periodontal abscess appears radiographically as a radiolucent {{c1::angular defect}} or {{c2::furcation radiolucency}}.
A periapical abscess is a radiolucency around the {{c1::apex}} of a tooth; do not mistake the {{c2::mental foramen}} near the apex of mandibular premolars for one.
Abscess, trauma or inflammation can cause {{c1::resorption}} of tooth structure.
The PDL space appears as a thin {{c1::radiolucent}} (black) line around the root; it is uniform in health, and a widened space indicates {{c2::trauma and/or infection}}.
Radiographs can detect some {{c1::interproximal}} calculus and overhanging restorations; deposits and overhangs on other surfaces usually are not visible.
Enamel pearls are most common in the {{c1::furcation areas of posterior teeth}} and can be mistaken for {{c2::calculus}}.
Ankylosis occurs mostly in {{c1::deciduous}} teeth; the tooth fails to erupt at the proper time and needs to be {{c2::extracted}}.
Impaction can be caused by {{c1::dense bone}}, {{c2::tooth malpositioning}} and {{c3::inadequate space}}; {{c4::third molars}} are commonly affected.
Radiographs cannot exactly identify furcation involvement because the {{c1::buccal and lingual}} alveolar bones are superimposed and root angles can mask defects.
By the time bone loss is evident on radiographs, periodontitis has progressed beyond its {{c1::early stages}}.
The {{c1::shape of a bony defect}} cannot be accurately identified on a radiograph; the beam may have to be realigned to "open" the area.
Radiographs do not reveal {{c1::soft tissue defects (periodontal pockets)}} or {{c2::tooth mobility}}.
Bone and tissue do not regenerate after nonsurgical periodontal therapy, so a realistic goal is {{c1::maintaining the current attachment level}}.
cloze.extra: Other goals: arrest progression (reduce inflammation, bleeding, plaque, probing depths; arrest bone loss).

cloze.text: Periodontal treatment goals also include preventing {{c1::recurrence}} and altering or eliminating contributing {{c2::risk factors}} such as smoking.
cloze.extra: Every patient responds differently, so the treatment plan and OHI may need adjusting (p.111).

cloze.text: McGuire (1991) prognosis "very good": less than {{c1::25%}} attachment loss.
McGuire prognosis "good": less than 25% attachment loss and/or {{c1::class I furcation}} involvement.
McGuire prognosis "fair": {{c1::25–50%}} attachment loss and/or class I furcation.
McGuire prognosis "poor": {{c1::50–75%}} attachment loss and/or class {{c2::II or III}} furcation, class {{c3::II}} mobility.
McGuire prognosis "hopeless": over {{c1::75%}} attachment loss, class {{c2::III}} mobility.
NSPT includes debridement/SRP, education, {{c1::adjunct therapy}} (chlorhexidine, antibiotics, etc.) and self-care instruction.
cloze.extra: It also covers control of infection and reinfection, reduction of inflammation, and systemic disease control.

cloze.text: NSPT is indicated for gingivitis, slight to moderate periodontitis, or patients who will undergo periodontal surgery; an oral prophylaxis is only for a {{c1::healthy periodontium}}.
cloze.extra: AAP 2017 terms: slight/moderate periodontitis ≈ Stage I/II.

cloze.text: A {{c1::periodontist}} should be involved in the success of periodontal treatment.
Pockets of {{c1::3–5 mm}} are a challenge for subgingival plaque removal.
Goal of NSPT: reduce pathogens, address risk factors (e.g., smoking) and arrest progression; usually {{c1::multiple appointments}} are required.

Root planing (outdated term) is designed to remove rough, calculus-impregnated {{c1::cementum or surface dentin}} to produce "glassy smooth" surfaces; practice is moving away from this to {{c2::preserve cementum}}.
Full mouth disinfection = debridement of all four quadrants within {{c1::24–48 hours}}.
In periodontal therapy, the educated patient is the {{c1::co-therapist}}.
cloze.extra: Educate on disease, risk factors, home care, nutrition, professional maintenance.

cloze.text: At non-responsive sites, check for {{c1::residual calculus or roughness}}, look for other factors (systemic disease, tobacco use) and consider periodontal surgery.
Adjunct therapy (lasers, antibiotics) is used {{c1::in addition to}} NSPT; alone it does not improve periodontal health.
{{c1::Periostat}} is doxycycline hyclate, a systemic {{c2::20 mg}} capsule taken orally (sub-antimicrobial dose).
Periostat works primarily by inhibiting {{c1::collagenase (MMP-8)}}.
Arestin and Atridox are derived from {{c1::tetracycline}} and are inserted into the pocket with a {{c2::blunt cannula}}; both dissolve, so no removal is needed.
After Arestin: do not brush for {{c1::12 hours}} and do not floss the site for {{c2::10 days}}; it is bacteriostatic for up to {{c3::14 days}}.
After Atridox: do not brush or floss the site for {{c1::7 days}}.
PerioChip dissolves, but may not fit well in pockets shallower than {{c1::5 mm}}; do not floss the site for {{c2::10 days}}.

Tetracycline HCl fibers are a saturated cord packed into the pocket and retained with {{c1::adhesive}}; they are not given to {{c2::pregnant women or children}} because of {{c3::tetracycline stain}} of developing teeth.
cloze.extra: Less commonly used now due to newer local delivery systems.

cloze.text: Periodontal maintenance is ongoing care at intervals of {{c1::3–4 months}} for patients with periodontal disease.
A {{c1::3-month}} maintenance interval suits patients who completed NSPT and have {{c2::poor}} oral hygiene.
A {{c1::4-month}} interval suits patients who completed NSPT with adequate oral hygiene and stable clinical attachment levels.
A {{c1::6-month to 1-year}} interval suits patients who maintain good home care and have stabilized oral health.
Once a patient is diagnosed with periodontal disease, subsequent recall appointments are always called {{c1::periodontal maintenance}}.
Periodontal surgery is indicated when {{c1::NSPT}} has not achieved the desired outcomes; goal: a healthy, comfortable, functional and esthetic oral environment.
In periodontal flap surgery the gums are lifted away from tooth and bone to allow access, then the gingival tissue is typically replaced in an {{c1::apical}} position.
cloze.extra: Goal: minimize pocket depth and allow thorough cleaning; indications: access for root debridement, removing diseased tissue, reshaping bone/gum.

cloze.text: A gum/connective tissue graft is indicated for {{c1::exposed roots}} (sensitivity, esthetics) or areas needing more gingival strength; tissue comes from a donor site such as the {{c2::palate}} or a donor source ({{c3::allograft}}).
cloze.extra: Covers root surfaces, reduces sensitivity, evens the gum line.

cloze.text: Gingival curettage removes the {{c1::soft tissue lining}} of periodontal pockets; it is used with SRP and is less common today as a standalone procedure.
Gingivectomy (surgical removal of gingival tissue) is indicated for pocket reduction and {{c1::gingival hyperplasia}}; it {{c2::does not}} involve bone reshaping.
Gingivoplasty reshapes the gingiva to correct {{c1::irregular gingival contours}} (e.g., tissue craters from necrotizing gingivitis); often done with a gingivectomy.
cloze.extra: The book says "NUG" — the AAP 2017 classification calls it necrotizing gingivitis (NG).

cloze.text: Osseous surgery reshapes alveolar bone by {{c1::osteoplasty}} (bone reshaping) and/or {{c2::ostectomy}} (bone removal); often combined with flap surgery and bone grafting.
Bone graft types: {{c1::autograft}} = patient's own bone; {{c2::allograft}} = human (cadaver) bone; {{c3::alloplastic}} = synthetic; {{c4::xenograft}} = animal bone, usually bovine.
cloze.extra: Prefixes: auto- = self; allo- = other (same species); xeno- = foreign (another species: bovine, porcine); alloplastic = synthetic/man-made.

cloze.text: In guided tissue regeneration (GTR) a {{c1::barrier membrane}} placed over the bone defect, under the gum, keeps faster-growing {{c2::soft tissue}} out so slower bone and ligament cells can repopulate it.
GTR aims to regenerate {{c1::bone and periodontal ligament}} in bone craters or defects.
Crown lengthening is indicated for an {{c1::insufficient clinical crown}} for restorative or cosmetic needs; it reshapes excess gum tissue and often the {{c2::underlying bone}}.
cloze.extra: Functional (expose tooth for a crown) or esthetic ("gummy smile").

cloze.text: Dental implants are typically made of {{c1::titanium}} and serve as anchors for prostheses.
An {{c1::endosteal}} implant is placed directly IN the bone; it is the {{c2::most common}} implant type (screws, cylinders, blades) and needs adequate bone volume.
A {{c1::subperiosteal}} implant sits on top of the jawbone under the periosteum, for minimal bone height; it is less common today due to advances in bone grafting.
A sinus lift (augmentation) raises the floor of the {{c1::maxillary sinus}} and places bone graft to allow implants in the {{c2::posterior maxilla}}.
After periodontal surgery some blood seeping is normal; the patient should not forcefully spit or rinse on the {{c1::first day}} because it may disturb {{c2::blood clotting}}.
After the first post-surgical day, rinse gently with {{c1::warm salt water}} (or a prescribed antimicrobial) and brush gently, avoiding the surgical area.
Use {{c1::ice}} to control post-surgical inflammation.
Post-surgical chlorhexidine rinse: {{c1::15 ml}} twice daily for {{c2::30 seconds}} (or as prescribed).
Chlorhexidine is effective against gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative bacteria and {{c1::fungi}}.

basic.front: How is the width of attached gingiva calculated?

basic.back: Pocket caused by gingival swelling/enlargement from inflammation — NO apical migration of the junctional epithelium and no loss of attachment
Opening for drainage of infection; may be visible as a small bulge on the gingiva
Palpable or visible movement of a tooth when in function
Loss of interradicular bone on multirooted teeth

basic.front: How is a plaque percentage score calculated, and what does a lower score mean?
basic.back: (# tooth surfaces with plaque ÷ total # surfaces) × 100; the lower the score, the less plaque
Loss of alveolar bone on the facial (rarely lingual) leaving an oval, root-exposed defect running apically from the CEJ
A "window" of bone loss on the facial or lingual that places the exposed root directly against gingiva or alveolar mucosa
Sheet of compact bone lining the socket next to the PDL; continuous white (radiopaque) line around the root following the PDL space
Mass of enamel on an abnormal surface such as a root
Fusion of the tooth (root cementum/dentin) with the adjacent alveolar bone
Tooth positioned against another structure so that it fails to erupt
Prediction of the duration, course and outcome of a disease
basic.extra: Influenced by patient compliance, systemic diseases, local factors (e.g., plaque level).

basic.front: How does periodontal debridement differ from root planing?
basic.back: Debridement removes plaque, its by-products and calculus only to the extent needed to restore periodontal health (balance of flora and host) — it does NOT include aggressive removal of cementum.
Ability of an agent to be released slowly over a long period of time (chlorhexidine has high substantivity)

typein.question: A probe reading falls at 3.5 mm. What is recorded (mm)?
typein.extra: Millimeter readings are rounded UP to the next whole number.

typein.question: Probing pressure should be between ___ grams (format: x–y).
How many probing readings are recorded per tooth?
Probing depth 4 mm; gingival margin 1 mm apical to the CEJ. CAL in mm?
Probing depth 6 mm; gingival margin 2 mm coronal to the CEJ. CAL in mm?
High kVp preferred for periodontal radiographs = at least how many kVp?
Pockets of ___ mm or deeper cannot be successfully treated with NSPT (residual calculus usually remains).
Re-evaluation is performed how many weeks after completing therapy? (x–y)

match.prompt: Match each osseous defect to its borders.
Match each Miller mobility class to its finding.
Match each Glickman furcation class to its charting symbol.
Match each McGuire prognosis to its criteria.
Match each adjunct product to its active ingredient.
Match each graft term to the source of its material.
Match each periodontal surgery to its main purpose.
pairs: Access for debridement; reduce pocket depth
Regenerate bone and PDL with a membrane

sort.prompt: Sort each feature: horizontal or vertical (angular) bone loss?
categories: Crest NOT parallel to CEJ–CEJ line

mcq.question: A patient taking a calcium channel blocker has 5 mm probing depths on the anterior teeth. The gingival margin is 5 mm coronal to the CEJ and the alveolar crest is 1–2 mm apical to the CEJ. These pockets are best described as:
mcq.explanation: The pocket is due entirely to gingival enlargement (CAL = 5 − 5 = 0): no apical migration of the junctional epithelium, so it is a pseudo(gingival) pocket. A suprabony pocket requires attachment loss with the base still above the crest.

mcq.question: On tooth #19 a furcation probe passes completely from the buccal to the lingual furcation, but the furcation entrance is covered by gingiva and not clinically visible. Using Glickman's classification this is:
mcq.explanation: Class III = probe passes completely through. Class IV also passes through, but the furcation entrance is clinically visible (gingival recession); here it is covered.

mcq.question: During flap surgery an oval area of exposed root is seen on the facial of #8. The defect is surrounded by bone, with an intact band of alveolar bone between it and the crest. This defect is a:
mcq.explanation: A fenestration is a window of bone loss bordered coronally by alveolar bone. A dehiscence extends from the CEJ apically with no coronal bone border.

mcq.question: Radiographs are useful in periodontal assessment for evaluating all of the following EXCEPT:
options: B. Widening of the PDL space
mcq.explanation: Pockets are soft tissue defects and are not visible radiographically (nor is mobility); they must be probed. Crest height, PDL width and interproximal calculus can be seen.

mcq.question: Minocycline microspheres were just placed in a 6 mm pocket on #14. Which post-op instruction is correct?
options: A. Do not brush or floss the site for 7 days
B. Do not brush for 12 hours; do not floss the site for 10 days
C. Return in 7–10 days to have the product removed
D. Do not floss the site for 10 days; brushing is unrestricted
mcq.answer: B. Do not brush for 12 hours; do not floss the site for 10 days
mcq.explanation: Arestin: no brushing for 12 h, no flossing at the site for 10 days; it dissolves (no removal). 7 days of no brushing/flossing is Atridox; floss-only restriction is PerioChip.

mcq.question: A patient completed NSPT 4 months ago. Today her oral hygiene is poor, with heavy plaque and bleeding. The most appropriate periodontal maintenance interval is:
mcq.explanation: Poor oral hygiene after NSPT → 3-month interval. 4 months is for adequate hygiene with stable attachment levels.

mcq.question: A patient dislikes her "gummy smile"; her maxillary anterior crowns look short although the teeth are sound. Which procedure exposes more natural tooth structure by reshaping gingiva and often bone?
mcq.explanation: Crown lengthening exposes more tooth for restorative access or esthetics. A connective tissue graft does the opposite — it covers exposed roots.

mcq.question: A patient wants an implant to replace #3. The radiograph shows only 4 mm of bone between the alveolar crest and the floor of the maxillary sinus. Which procedure is most likely needed first?
mcq.explanation: Insufficient bone in the posterior maxilla due to sinus proximity → sinus lift with bone graft to create volume for an endosteal implant. Subperiosteal implants are now uncommon because grafting makes endosteal placement possible.

mcq.question: Which instruction is correct for a patient on the evening of periodontal flap surgery?
options: A. Rinse vigorously with salt water every 2 hours
B. Avoid forceful spitting or rinsing today
C. Apply heat to the face to reduce swelling
D. Brush the surgical site firmly to remove blood
mcq.answer: B. Avoid forceful spitting or rinsing today
mcq.explanation: Forceful spitting/rinsing on day 1 can disturb the clot; gentle warm salt-water rinses start after the first day. Ice (not heat) controls inflammation.

mcq.question: Which structure of the periodontium connects the cementum to the alveolar bone?
mcq.explanation: The periodontal ligament (PDL) fibers physically attach the tooth's cementum to the alveolar bone, providing support and proprioception.

mcq.question: Horizontal bone loss typically appears radiographically as:
options: A. Uniform reduction in bone height perpendicular to the tooth surface
B. Angular, trench-like bone loss between teeth
mcq.answer: A. Uniform reduction in bone height perpendicular to the tooth surface
mcq.explanation: Horizontal bone loss shows a uniform, flat loss of alveolar bone height along a line perpendicular to the long axis of the teeth.

mcq.question: A patient has 5 mm probing depths with recession of 2 mm. What is the clinical attachment level (CAL)?
mcq.explanation: CAL = probing depth + gingival recession. In this case: 5 mm + 2 mm = 7 mm of attachment loss.

mcq.question: Which condition is characterized by punched-out papillae, pain, spontaneous bleeding, and a fetid odor?
mcq.explanation: Necrotizing gingivitis (NG) presents with distinct clinical signs: painful ulcerated papillae, metallic taste, spontaneous bleeding, and a foul odor due to necrosis and anaerobic bacteria.

mcq.question: A patient has generalized Stage III, Grade B periodontitis. What does Grade B indicate?
options: A. Stable disease with no loss over 5 years
B. Rapid bone loss and high risk factors
C. Moderate progression with risk factors such as smoking or diabetes
D. Early onset of attachment loss
mcq.answer: C. Moderate progression with risk factors such as smoking or diabetes
mcq.explanation: Grade B reflects moderate disease progression, often in patients with identifiable risk factors like <10 cigarettes/day or controlled diabetes.

mcq.question: Which tissue of the periodontium is keratinized and resistant to mechanical forces?
mcq.explanation: The attached gingiva is keratinized and provides mechanical protection against forces of mastication. Alveolar mucosa is non-keratinized.

mcq.question: Vertical bone loss is typically associated with:
options: A. Stage I and II periodontitis
mcq.explanation: Vertical (angular) bone loss creates bony defects below the crest of the alveolar bone, commonly forming infrabony pockets.

mcq.question: The first clinical sign of gingival inflammation is usually:
mcq.explanation: Bleeding on probing is often the earliest detectable sign of gingival inflammation, even before obvious color or contour changes.

mcq.question: Which bacteria is most associated with necrotizing periodontal diseases?
mcq.explanation: Spirochetes, especially T. denticola, are strongly linked to necrotizing periodontal diseases due to their tissue invasiveness and anaerobic nature.

mcq.question: In staging periodontitis, Stage IV may include all of the following, EXCEPT:
options: C. Bone loss limited to the coronal third
D. Clinical attachment loss of 5 mm or greater
mcq.answer: C. Bone loss limited to the coronal third
mcq.explanation: Stage IV periodontitis involves advanced destruction, including mid-root or apical bone loss, mobility, and functional instability. Coronal third bone loss is typical of earlier stages.

mcq.question: Which part of the periodontium is responsible for sensing pressure and pain during mastication?
mcq.explanation: The periodontal ligament (PDL) contains sensory fibers that detect pressure, pain, and proprioception during chewing and movement.

mcq.question: What is the CAL if the probing depth is 4 mm and the gingival margin is 2 mm coronal to the CEJ?
options: D. Cannot be calculated without radiographs
mcq.explanation: If the gingival margin is coronal to the CEJ, subtract that amount from the probing depth: 4 mm − 2 mm = 2 mm CAL.

mcq.question: Which term describes the extension of inflammation from the gingiva into the connective tissue and alveolar bone?
mcq.explanation: Periodontitis is characterized by the spread of inflammation into the deeper supporting tissues, leading to attachment and bone loss.

mcq.question: In necrotizing periodontitis (NP), what additional clinical feature distinguishes it from necrotizing gingivitis (NG)?
mcq.explanation: NP includes all features of NG plus loss of attachment and alveolar bone, making it more destructive and severe.

mcq.question: A 30-year-old patient presents with rapid bone loss, minimal plaque, and no systemic conditions. What is the most appropriate Grade classification?
options: D. Cannot be determined without mobility data
mcq.explanation: Grade C is assigned when there is rapid progression of periodontitis, especially in younger patients, with minimal local factors and no clear systemic contributors.
